response.answer: Alternative retirement ages and replacement rates increase income inequality and wealth concentration among older adults, reshaping long-run age-specific Gini and top-1% share trajectories in Central and Eastern European countries. Higher retirement ages extend working careers, while higher replacement rates boost income for retirees.

results.title: How Raising Pilot Retirement Ages Could Reshape Airline Costs and Industry Valuations
results.content: # How Raising Pilot Retirement Ages Could Reshape Airline Costs and Industry Valuations. - IATA proposes raising global pilot retirement age to 67, with Japan/Canada already testing higher thresholds, sparking debates over cost, safety, and labor impacts. - Extended careers could cut training costs but increase medical/monitoring expenses, as aging pilots show higher safety deviations per ScienceDirect studies. - Pilot unions oppose age extensions due to safety risks, while countries like Japan use mentorship programs to balance experience with workforce development. The aviation industry is at a crossroads as regulators, airlines, and pilot unions clash over the future of pilot retirement ages. With the International Air Transport Association (IATA) pushing to raise the global retirement age from 65 to 67 and countries like Japan and Canada already experimenting with higher thresholds, investors must grapple with how these shifts could redefine operational costs, safety dynamics, and ultimately, airline valuations. Raising the retirement age could significantly reduce the frequency of pilot training and recruitment cycles, which are among the most expensive operational expenses for airlines. According to a report by *AeroTime*, Japan's decision to extend the retirement age to 68 has allowed carriers like All Nippon Airways to retain seasoned pilots, easing the pressure to train replacementsICAO considers raising pilot retirement age - AeroTime[1]. A study published in *ScienceDirect* found that commercial pilots in China exhibited higher exceedance rates (deviations from safe flight parameters) as they aged past 65, suggesting that airlines might need to invest in enhanced monitoring systems or mentorship programsEffects of age and flight exposure on flight safety performance[3]. The (ALPA) and Allied Pilots Association have fiercely opposed age extensions, arguing that insufficient data exists on the risks of pilots in their late 60sIATA considers raising pilot retirement age - AeroTime[4]. For investors, the key question is whether the perceived safety benefits of experienced pilots outweigh the financial and operational risks of aging crews. Conversely, countries like Japan have reported smoother transitions by pairing age extensions with mentorship programs that pair older and younger pilotsICAO considers raising pilot retirement age - AeroTime[1]. For investors, the stakes are clear: Raising pilot retirement ages could unlock cost savings and address labor shortages, but it also introduces safety and regulatory risks.

results.title: Replacement Rates: How Social Security and the Private Retirement System Work Together
results.content: In this study, the Employee Benefit Research Institute’s Retirement Security Projection Model® (RSPM) is used to show how these components work together by calculating the expected replacement rate of each source and the resulting combined replacement rate. Examining how much each of these sources replace retirees’ average preretirement earnings shows that Social Security provides a larger share of income in retirement for those who earned less, while those who earned more can expect more from the DC system. * The share of replaced income from Social Security is larger for those with lower incomes, while the share from DC/individual retirement account (IRA) assets is larger for those with higher incomes. At a retirement age of 67, the replacement rates of both DC/IRA assets and Social Security increase by 5–7 percentage points compared with a retirement age of 65. Even if Social Security benefits or the annuity value of the DC/IRA assets are changed, the same pattern emerges of the two components combined providing similar replacement rates across all incomes.

results.title: How Do Retirement Ages Affect Retirement? | NBER
results.content: Facing rising life expectancies and falling birth rates, many countries have raised retirement ages in their public pension programs to ameliorate long-run fiscal deficits. Public pension retirement ages — including the early retirement age (ERA) when benefits are first available and the normal retirement age (NRA) around which the benefit calculation is centered — may influence workers' decisions of when to exit the labor force. While there may be changes in the financial incentive for continued work that occurs at these ages, past research suggests that these changes alone are insufficient to explain the increase in retirement. While there are many instances of countries changing the early or normal retirement age in their pension plan, these reforms typically include other changes that can also affect work incentives and behavior. In **Relabeling, Retirement and Regret** (NBER RDRC Working Paper NB19-20 and NBER Working Paper 27534), researchers Jonathan Gruber, Ohto Kanninen, and Terhi Ravaska explore this question in the context of a major pension reform in Finland. Importantly, the reform included a major relabeling of pension retirement ages that was accompanied by modest and continuous changes in financial incentives, enabling the researchers to identify workers' retirement responses to pension retirement ages. Workers who were 63 at the time of reform also experienced changes in both retirement ages and financial incentives. By contrast, workers who were age 64 at the time of the reform were unaffected by the access to new retirement option, since they could already anticipate having access to normal retirement benefits at age 65, but had similar changes in financial incentives. Comparing these groups of workers allows the researchers to isolate the effect of relabeling age 63 as a focal retirement age. This extremely large and immediate response to the relabeling of age 63 as the new normal retirement age suggests that "relabeling is as powerful as enormous changes in pension wealth or dynamic pension retirement incentives" in driving retirement decisions. The authors also explore regret: whether pension retirement ages affect the decision to return to work.

results.title: Retirement Trajectories and Health in Japan | Demography | Duke University Press
results.content: # Retirement Trajectories and Health in Japan. Raymo; Retirement Trajectories and Health in Japan. The relationship between retirement and health is a critical issue in rapidly aging societies. Numerous studies have investigated the effect of retirement on subsequent health, but this research has paid little attention to heterogeneous patterns of retirement. To address this limitation, we examine the relationship between retirement pathways from full-time regular employment and health. Using the 2005–2019 Longitudinal Survey of Middle-aged and Elderly Persons conducted in Japan, the world's oldest country, we first use sequence analysis to identify distinct retirement trajectories at ages 59–66. We then evaluate alternative approaches to estimate relationships between these retirement trajectories and an index measure of self-rated health. Results of ordinary least-squares and inverse probability-weighted regression adjustment models show that both gradual and abrupt retirement are associated with worse health relative to continued regular employment. In contrast, estimates from instrumental variable models are imprecise and provide no clear evidence of a relationship between retirement trajectories and health. Retirement, Health, Trajectory analysis, Japan.
